missions/american-baptist-burma-mission/: Adoniram Judson and the American Baptist mission to Burma and the Karen
modern-missions
Rangoon (Yangon), Burma
transformed

Foreign missionaries were expelled by Ne Win's government in 1966, but the mission had long since become the Myanmar Baptist Convention (founded 1865 as the Burma Baptist Missionary Convention), now one of the largest Baptist bodies in Asia, overwhelmingly among Karen, Kachin, Chin and other minority peoples. The sending body continues as American Baptist International Ministries.

Begun when Adoniram and Ann Judson, sent by the American Board, became Baptists en route to India and settled in Rangoon in 1813. The mission produced the Burmese Bible and dictionary but few Burman Buddhist converts; its great growth came among the Karen after the conversion of Ko Tha Byu (1828), and later among the Kachin, Chin and peoples of Northeast India. It also galvanised American Baptists to organise nationally (1814) for foreign mission.

Adoniram Judson (1788–1850), son of a Congregational minister and one of the Andover students who prompted the founding of the American Board, sailed for India in February 1812 with his wife Ann Hasseltine Judson. Anticipating a meeting with William Carey's Baptists at Serampore, he studied the question of baptism on the voyage and became convinced of believer's baptism by immersion; the Judsons were baptised by William Ward in Calcutta in September 1812 and their colleague Luther Rice soon followed. Resigning from the Board, they appealed to American Baptists for support. Rice returned home to organise it, and in May 1814 Baptists met in Philadelphia to form the General Missionary Convention of the Baptist Denomination (the 'Triennial Convention') — the first national Baptist body in America, created for the sake of foreign mission.

Expelled from British India by the East India Company, the Judsons went via Mauritius and Madras to Rangoon, then under the Burmese king, arriving in July 1813 and taking over the house of Felix Carey. Judson spent years mastering Burmese and Pali and adopted the Buddhist device of a zayat, a roadside shelter for discussion; the first Burman convert, Maung Nau, was baptised only in June 1819. When the First Anglo-Burmese War broke out in 1824, Judson was imprisoned as a suspected spy at Ava and Oung-pen-la for about seventeen months, in fetters and near death; Ann's tireless advocacy and her letters home made the couple celebrities in America. She died at Amherst in 1826. Judson completed the Burmese Bible in 1834, revised it in 1840 and compiled an English–Burmese dictionary (1849); his translation remains in use. He died at sea in 1850. His three wives — Ann, Sarah Boardman and Emily Chubbuck — each wrote widely read works that made the Judson family central to American missionary piety.

Buddhist Burmans proved largely resistant, but the hill and plains Karen responded dramatically. In 1828 George Dana Boardman baptised Ko Tha Byu, a former robber and debtor slave, at Tavoy; he became an indefatigable evangelist among his own people. Many Karen held a tradition of a 'lost book' that their elder brother, the white foreigner, would one day restore, and of a creator god Y'wa; missionaries and Karen evangelists alike read the Bible as the fulfilment of these traditions. Jonathan Wade devised a Sgaw Karen script around 1832, Francis Mason translated the Bible, and a Karen theological seminary opened in 1845. Karen churches quickly became self-supporting and sent their own missionaries to other hill peoples.

From Burma American Baptists spread into Assam (1836), where Nathan Brown and later Miles Bronson and Edward Clark began work that led to the Naga and Garo churches, and into the Telugu country of South India, where the 'Lone Star' mission at Nellore (1836) became the scene of the Ongole mass movement of 1878, when John Clough's colleagues baptised about 2,200 Madigas in a single day. In Burma itself Ola Hanson created a script for the Kachin (Jingpho) language and completed the Kachin Bible in 1927, and Arthur and Laura Carson opened work among the Chin at Haka in 1899. Rangoon Baptist College (1872, later Judson College) became a pillar of higher education.

The mission's success among minorities had political consequences. The British annexed Burma in three wars (1824–26, 1852, 1885); Christian Karen, Kachin and Chin served in disproportionate numbers in the colonial army and police, and Burman nationalists came to associate Christianity with the minorities and with British rule. After independence in 1948 the Karen National Union took up arms in 1949, beginning one of the world's longest-running conflicts; many Karen Christians were among its leaders and many more among its victims and refugees. In 1966 the military government expelled the remaining foreign missionaries and nationalised mission schools. American Baptists, meanwhile, had split in 1845 over slavery, the southern churches forming the Southern Baptist Convention and the northern the American Baptist Missionary Union, which inherited the Burma mission.

Self-governing since the founding of the Burma Baptist Missionary Convention in 1865, the churches survived the expulsion of missionaries and grew strongly under national leadership. The Myanmar Baptist Convention reports well over a million members in more than a dozen language conventions, and Kachin and Chin states are now majority Christian. Judson's Bible and Ko Tha Byu's legacy remain central to the identity of Christians in a Buddhist-majority country where they face periodic discrimination and, in minority regions, the violence of civil war.

A mission that won few Burman Buddhists but became the seedbed of mass Christian movements among the Karen, Kachin and Chin and, through its offshoots, in Northeast India and Andhra. The Myanmar Baptist Convention, self-governing since 1865 and without foreign missionaries since 1966, is the mission's principal legacy.
